q: Which statement about UTI in young children is FALSE?
o: After 1 year UTIs are commoner in girls
Fever is the main presenting sign after infancy
Vomiting is a specific sign of UTI
Boys have more UTIs in the first year
e: After the neonatal period fever is the main symptom; vomiting is nonspecific for UTI at 0–24 months. Boys outnumber girls under 1 year; after that girls do, lifelong. Risk in girls: white race, age <12 months, temperature ≥39°C, fever ≥2 days, no other source (≥2 factors: ≥1%, ≥3: ≥2%; African American race lowers risk). Under 6 years, recurrence is 12% per year after a UTI. Clinical symptoms correlate poorly with localisation.
b: Fever is main sign after neonatal period

q: Which statement about Peyronie disease (PD) is FALSE?
o: It is a wound-healing disorder of the tunica
Most plaques are dorsal, near the septum
e: PD is not premalignant. It is an abnormal wound-healing response in the tunica albuginea after injury (delamination between layers). 60–70% of plaques are dorsal near the septum. Improvement in ≤13%; full resolution is very rare; up to 50% worsen untreated. Incidence 3–9%, peak age 50; diabetes in 33%. Acute phase then stable phase (typically 12 months from onset and 6 months stable curvature).

q: Circumcision reduces UTI in the first 6 months of life by about:
e: Uropathogen colonisation of the prepuce peaks in the first 6 months and falls by 5 years.

q: A man with clinical stage I NSGCT and lymphovascular invasion had a scrotal orchiectomy. The best management is:
o: RPLND plus scar and cord excision
e: Scrotal violation plus vascular invasion makes surveillance suboptimal; RPLND with wide scar and cord excision. RPLND is the treatment of choice for stage I NSGCT with teratoma. Offer sperm banking before any RPLND. Small-volume pN1 is cured by RPLND alone in ~70%.
b: Scrotal violation + LVI: RPLND, excise scar and cord
RPLND first choice for stage I with teratoma

q: Which statement about stone epidemiology is FALSE?
o: Peak incidence is in the 4th to 6th decades
Stones are commonest in African Americans
Stones are 2–3 times commoner in men
Prevalence correlates with body mass index
e: Whites have the highest prevalence; lowest in African American men and (one series) Asian women. Calcium oxalate stones are most prevalent in the US southeast. Men 2–3×; uncommon before 20; peak 4th–6th decades. Metabolic syndrome raises risk; high BMI raises oxalate, uric acid, sodium and phosphorus excretion and uric acid supersaturation. Incidence is rising worldwide.
b: Rises with BMI and metabolic syndrome

q: After radical prostatectomy, Peyronie-type penile fibrosis develops in about:
e: Tal 2010: 15.9% at mean 13.9 months; Ciancio: 11% fibrosis, with curvature 93%, waistband deformity 24%, palpable plaques 69%.

q: Which statement about renal cryoablation is FALSE?
o: −40°C lies about 3 mm inside the ice edge
The ice ball extends 5–10 mm past the tumour
A single freeze–thaw cycle is preferred
e: A double freeze-thaw cycle (holding −40°C) gives better ablation than a single cycle. Normal parenchyma dies at −19.4°C, but tumour needs −40°C, reached 3.1 mm inside the ice ball edge, so extend the ice 5–10 mm beyond the tumour. Haemorrhage is the commonest complication of cryoablation.

q: A man with complete T10 spinal cord injury, after spinal shock, most likely shows:
o: Areflexia with an open bladder neck
DO with both sphincters in synergy
e: Complete lesions between T6 and S2 (above sacral cord, below sympathetic outflow): involuntary contractions without sensation, smooth sphincter synergy, striated sphincter dyssynergia. Lesions at or above T6 (cord T7–T8) may add smooth sphincter dyssynergia and autonomic hyperreflexia. Suprapontine lesions: DO with synergic sphincters and preserved sensation. Neurological examination is no substitute for urodynamics.

q: The superior limit of a standard RPLND template is:
e: Templates do not include nodes above the renal hilum, so retrocrural nodes are outside them.

q: Which statement about staging muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) is FALSE?
o: About 25% of cT2 tumours have nodes at cystectomy
Repeat TUR is advised for T1 high grade
Bimanual EUA is part of local staging
e: Laterality of a single positive node has no prognostic value (number of nodes may). About 25% of cT2 have node metastases; 70–80% of node-positive patients recur. Staging: adequate TURBT, EUA, cross-sectional imaging, labs. Re-resect T1G3 (understaging common). Fat may occur within the bladder wall (not perivesical). Node risk rises with depth and LVI; skip nodal metastases are rare (unlike prostate cancer).
b: Laterality of single node: no prognostic value

q: Which statement about PSA is FALSE?
o: PSA is specific to prostate cancer
Its serum half-life is 2 to 3 days
e: PSA is organ-specific, not disease-specific: inflammation and BPH raise it too. It is a kallikrein (as is hK2, which is more intensely expressed in cancer, especially poorly differentiated). Half-life 2–3 days. Gram for gram, cancer cells make less PSA (up to 1.5-fold lower mRNA); serum rises from architectural disruption. Expression is androgen-driven. Ectopic PSA occurs in breast, adrenal and renal cancers. Up to 30% with raised PSA have cancer on biopsy; 75–80% do not.
b: Cancer cells make less PSA per gram

q: Which statement about perioperative chemotherapy for MIBC (per the book) is TRUE?
o: Adjuvant data are stronger than neoadjuvant
e: Most single trials were not definitive, but meta-analysis shows a small (about 5%) survival advantage for neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy; adjuvant evidence is weaker.

q: Which statement about urine dipstick tests in children is FALSE?
o: First morning urine best detects nitrite
Nitrite is highly sensitive but not specific
Leukocyte esterase is sensitive, less specific
e: Nitrite is highly specific but insensitive: gram-negative enteric bacteria need hours to reduce nitrate, so infants' frequent voiding and dilute urine give false negatives; urinary retention would not. Leukocyte esterase: high sensitivity, low specificity. >5–10 WBC/HPF suggests UTI; culture confirms. CRP and procalcitonin rise in pyelonephritis.
b: First morning urine best for nitrite

q: Which statement about evaluating Peyronie disease is FALSE?
o: Calcification can occur early in the disease
Calliper plaque size is accurate and useful
Duplex after injection best measures curvature
e: Plaque size is inaccurate by any method (not a discrete lesion). Calcification may occur early; it does not mean mature disease, and it reduces success of verapamil or interferon injections. Duplex after vasoactive injection: calcification, vascular parameters, erectile response vs home erection and objective deformity (not sensation). Distress in 77–94%; shortening and inability to have intercourse drive it; partners are affected too. After prostatectomy 11–16% develop PD/fibrosis.
b: Duplex after injection: best curvature assessment

q: Which commercial test uses 31 cell-cycle progression genes?
e: Prolaris: 31 CCP + 15 housekeeping genes (progression and death). Oncotype DX: 12 genes in 4 pathways + 5 housekeeping (adverse pathology). Decipher: 22-marker classifier.

q: Which statement about laparoscopic RPLND is FALSE?
o: It improves disease-free survival over open
Bleeding is the commonest cause of conversion
Lumbar veins lie close to sympathetic nerves
e: No study shows a disease-free survival difference between open and laparoscopic RPLND. Vascular injury is the commonest intraoperative complication and bleeding the commonest reason to convert (<5% in experienced hands). Chylous ascites (<2%): low-fat diet, hydration, drainage; reoperation last. Nerve-sparing: take care around lumbar veins next to the sympathetic chain. If a suspicious node is found, do a full bilateral dissection (chemo won't compensate). Templates do not extend above the renal hilum (no retrocrural nodes).
b: No DFS difference open vs laparoscopic
Lumbar veins next to sympathetic chain

q: Which statement about crystallisation is FALSE?
o: Homogeneous nucleation needs an impurity surface
Matrix makes up about 2.5% of a typical stone
Metastable urine is supersaturated without precipitating
Most stone salts are supersaturated in urine
e: Homogeneous nucleation is nucleus formation in pure solution; heterogeneous nucleation uses impurities as a surface. Concentration product = product of concentrations; solubility product = where precipitation can occur; above it, a solution is supersaturated; if it does not precipitate it is metastable; precipitation occurs at the formation product. Most salts are supersaturated; inhibitors keep them in solution. Matrix (mucoproteins, carbohydrates, inhibitors) is ~2.5% (range 2.5–65% by type). Saturation index (EQUIL 2; JESS more accurate) indicates stone-forming propensity.
b: Most salts supersaturated; inhibitors hold them

q: Without treatment, Peyronie curvature worsens in up to:
e: No more than 13% improve; full resolution is rare. Stable phase: about 12 months from onset with 6 months of unchanged curvature.

q: Which statement about radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is FALSE?
o: Collecting system injury is a serious risk
It bleeds more often than cryoablation
Real-time monitoring is its main drawback
e: Bleeding is more frequent with cryoablation. RFA heats by ionic agitation; charring raises impedance and blocks conduction, so probes are cooled or conductive saline used (a larger 'virtual electrode'). Its main drawback is difficulty monitoring in real time. Ureteral/collecting system injury is a serious RFA complication. RFA can be laparoscopic, percutaneous or open; CSS equals cryoablation. HIFU often causes skin burns.

q: Which statement about autonomic dysreflexia is FALSE?
o: First treatment is emptying the bladder
It causes pounding headache and hypertension
Sweating and flushing occur above the lesion
Tachycardia is the usual heart rate change
e: Exaggerated sympathetic response to stimuli below the lesion (at or above T6): pounding headache, hypertension, flushing and sweating above the lesion; bradycardia usual, arrhythmias possible. Remove the stimulus (empty the bladder), then 2% nitroglycerin paste above the lesion if needed.

q: Compared with partial nephrectomy, thermal ablation of small renal masses shows:
o: Equal local recurrence and better renal function
e: Meta-analyses: ablation has higher local recurrence, but metastasis-free and cancer-specific survival are comparable; studies are small and heterogeneous. Update: AUA 2021 lists thermal ablation as an option mainly for tumours under 3 cm, with biopsy beforehand.
b: AUA 2021: ablation option for <3 cm, biopsy first

q: Which statement about orthotopic neobladder in MIBC is FALSE?
o: A positive urethral margin bars a neobladder
Bladder neck biopsy is a surrogate in women
Anterior vaginal wall tumour bars it in women
e: The only contraindication in men is a positive apical urethral margin that cannot be cleared. In women, anterior vaginal wall, bladder neck or urethral involvement precludes it; the distal two-thirds of the urethra can provide continence; bladder neck biopsy substitutes for urethral biopsy. Age is not a contraindication with good pelvic support. Prostatic urethral CIS is commonest from mid-prostate to verumontanum at 5 and 7 o'clock (biopsy there); prostatic stromal invasion carries high recurrence risk. Ureteral margin status predicts upper tract recurrence.
b: Positive apical urethral margin: no neobladder
Anterior vaginal wall tumour: no neobladder
Women: bladder neck biopsy as surrogate

q: Which statement about PSA isoforms is FALSE?
o: Most complexed PSA is bound to ACT
Cancer raises the free PSA fraction
e: PSA from cancer escapes proteolytic processing, so more is complexed to α1-antichymotrypsin (ACT) and free PSA % is lower. ~70% of serum PSA is bound (α2-macroglobulin, API, ACT); ACT-PSA dominates and is higher in cancer. %fPSA is FDA-approved with benign DRE and PSA 4–10 ng/mL. Finasteride lowers total and free PSA by ~50% after 6 months (double the value: 4 → 8 ng/mL), leaving %fPSA unchanged. ProPSA ([−7]pPSA has a 7-amino-acid leader; hK2 cleaves it to active PSA) helps detection.

q: The classic urodynamic finding in end-stage diabetic cystopathy is:
e: Sensory and motor neuropathy: impaired sensation, increased capacity, decreased contractility and flow, later increased residual. In men, exclude outlet obstruction.

q: Which statement about imaging in paediatric UTI is FALSE?
o: DMSA is positive in only 50–66% of clinical APN
DMSA binds the glomerular basement membrane
Ultrasound is needed if fever lasts >48 h on therapy
CT is most accurate for renal abscess
e: DMSA binds proximal tubular cells and is excreted slowly, giving stable cortical images. 90% defervesce within 48 h; persisting fever needs renal/bladder US. Acute DMSA changes are the gold standard for pyelonephritis, positive in only 50–66% of clinically diagnosed cases. Renal abscess: urine culture negative in up to 20%; US detects ≥1 cm; CT is most sensitive and specific. Dysplasia with VUR can mimic scarring on DMSA. Scars are polar (compound papillae).
b: DMSA binds proximal tubule, not GBM
DMSA positive in 50–66% of clinical APN

q: A 30-year-old has mild PD with 15° curvature and mild pain. Best management:
e: Minimal disease may not worsen; collagenase is for 30–90°, oral agents are unproven, steroids lack evidence. Pentoxifylline is a nonspecific PDE inhibitor with anti-inflammatory/antifibrotic effects; iNOS-derived nitric oxide reduces reactive oxygen species and myofibroblasts, lowering collagen I. Intracavernosal injections do not cause PD (may cause fibrosis, pain, priapism).
b: Oral agents unproven; steroids no evidence

q: Which factor most strongly predicts survival after radical cystectomy?
e: Node status is a powerful predictor; 70–80% of node-positive patients recur.

q: Late relapse of a germ cell tumour (over 2 years after therapy) most often shows:
e: Teratoma's slow growth and chemoresistance explain late relapse. Viable GCT completely resected at post-chemotherapy RPLND: two more cycles of platinum-based chemotherapy improve survival (Einhorn: only 2/22 survived without it).

q: Which statement about stone inhibitors and promoters is FALSE?
o: Uric acid is a natural stone inhibitor
e: Uric acid promotes calcium oxalate stones (removes inhibitors, salting out, epitaxy/heterogeneous nucleation by sodium urate). Citrate complexes calcium (main action), inhibits nucleation, agglomeration and growth, enhances Tamm-Horsfall protein, and blocks urate-induced nucleation. Magnesium complexes oxalate; low magnesium accompanies low citrate. Nephrocalcin inhibits nucleation, growth, aggregation; Tamm-Horsfall inhibits aggregation; osteopontin inhibits growth, nucleation and aggregation. Nanobacteria have been implicated as niduses.

q: A man on finasteride for 1 year has PSA 4 ng/mL. His 'adjusted' PSA is about:
e: 5α-reductase inhibitors lower PSA by ~50% after 6 months; double the value. Saw palmetto does not affect PSA.

q: Which follow-up finding indicates successful renal tumour ablation?
o: No change in enhancement at 3 months
No enhancement, stable or smaller size
e: Complete loss of contrast enhancement on CT/MRI indicates destruction. Cryoablated lesions shrink ~50% in a year; RFA lesions may not shrink (later slight reduction and cavitation). Any growth is ominous. Biopsy before ablation to confirm malignancy. Ablation has higher local recurrence than surgery, but metastasis-free survival and CSS are similar; data are limited. Partial nephrectomy is the gold standard (equal oncology to radical, better renal function).
b: Cryo lesions shrink ~50% in a year
Any growth is ominous; biopsy first

q: Which statement about LUT dysfunction in brain disease is FALSE?
o: Detrusor overactivity is commonest after stroke
Prostatism after stroke needs urodynamics first
e: Multiple system atrophy commonly has sphincteric insufficiency (outlet surgery rarely indicated; poor compliance possible); Parkinson disease rarely does. Stroke: long-term DO with intact sensation. Parkinson: DO from loss of basal ganglia inhibition (substantia nigra). Before prostatectomy after stroke, full urodynamics excludes DO with impaired contractility. Cerebral palsy: most have normal storage/emptying; if abnormal, DO with coordinated sphincters (suprapontine); acute change in adult CP is usually unrelated. MS: DO with smooth synergia, intact sensation; may have striated dyssynergia or poor contractility. Progressive diseases damage upper tracts less than SCI.

q: Which is NOT a risk factor for UTI in a febrile girl (Gorelick)?
e: Risk factors: white race, age <12 months, temperature ≥39°C, fever ≥2 days, no other source. Two or more factors give ≥1% probability; three or more ≥2%.
b: White, <12 months, ≥39°C, fever ≥2 days, no source

q: Which statement about chemotherapy for MIBC is FALSE?
o: GC matches MVAC efficacy with less toxicity
Poor PS and visceral metastases predict poor outcome
e: Carboplatin is not first-line; cisplatin-ineligible patients should go straight to cystectomy. Gemcitabine-cisplatin vs MVAC (von der Maase): equal response (49% vs 46%) and survival (13.8 vs 14.8 months) with less toxicity. MSKCC: KPS <80% and visceral metastases predict poor outcome (median 33, 13.4, 9.3 months with 0, 1, 2 factors). Cisplatin-unfit: poor PS, CrCl <60, hearing loss, neuropathy, heart failure. Adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy may be considered (meta-analysis 9% OS benefit; trials weak). Updates: CheckMate 274 (adjuvant nivolumab); NIAGARA (2024, perioperative durvalumab with GC); EV-302 for metastatic disease.
b: Carboplatin not a cisplatin substitute neoadjuvantly
Poor PS and visceral mets: poor outcome

q: Which statement about prostate cancer molecular markers is FALSE?
o: PCA3 is a noncoding RNA on 9q21–22
TMPRSS2:ERG is in most screened cancers
PCA3 and the fusion can be combined in urine
e: TMPRSS2:ERG is an early event, nearly 100% specific, but present in only ~50% of PSA-screened cancers. PCA3 is noncoding (alternatively spliced, many stop codons, no open reading frame), measured in urine and combinable with the fusion. Hypermethylated genes: GSTP1, APC, RARβ2, RASSF1A. Tissue signatures (Prolaris 31 CCP + 15 housekeeping genes; Oncotype DX 12 + 5; Decipher 22 markers) add prognostic information on small FFPE samples. CTCs and ctDNA are promising in advanced disease.

q: Hypocitraturia is defined (book) as urinary citrate below:
e: Acidosis lowers citrate excretion; low magnesium often accompanies low citrate.

q: Which statement about UTI organisms and antibiotics in children is FALSE?
o: E. coli causes over 80% of UTIs
e: Nitrofurantoin has poor tissue penetration (not for febrile UTI) and is avoided in G6PD deficiency. E. coli >80%. Neonates: cover Enterococcus (ampicillin, first-generation cephalosporins). TMP-SMX displaces bilirubin (kernicterus) in prematures and <6 weeks. Febrile UTI in newborns: admit for IV antibiotics; febrile UTI 7–14 days, afebrile cystitis 2–4 days. Adenovirus causes viral haemorrhagic cystitis. Urethritis: gonorrhoea, Chlamydia, Ureaplasma; teenage STIs can cause PID, infertility and pelvic pain.
b: Nitrofurantoin not for febrile UTI (or G6PD)

q: Which statement about Peyronie surgery is FALSE?
o: Poor erections with PD favour a prosthesis
Plication carries the least risk of new ED
Ventral curves grafted risk more complete ED
Grafting suits poor rigidity, big curve
e: Poor rigidity absolutely contraindicates grafting; such men (or those failing high-dose duplex response) should have an IPP with straightening (manual modelling risks distal urethral/meatal injury). Plication is preferred for less severe curves: least cavernosal injury and ED, though more length loss. Grafting: strong erections with >70° curve, hinge, hourglass or short penis; main risk is postoperative ED (worse with ventral curves). Operate ≥1 year from onset with 6 months stable. Preoperative erectile function predicts outcome. No procedure increases length; grafting loses less than plication.
b: Plication: least ED risk, more length loss

q: Hyperuricosuria is defined (book) as uric acid excretion above:
e: Hyperuricosuria promotes sodium urate formation and calcium oxalate stones by heterogeneous nucleation.

q: Which statement about calcium metabolism and stones is FALSE?
e: 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 most potently stimulates intestinal calcium absorption (small bowel, intake-dependent). Hypercalciuria (>4 mg/kg/day) is the commonest abnormality: absorptive (raised absorption after oral load; vitamin D receptor changes), renal (tubular leak, secondary hyperparathyroidism), resorptive (hyperparathyroidism; thiazides worsen hypercalcaemia). PTH increases tubular calcium reabsorption and phosphate excretion. PTH-like hormone from lung, breast, renal, penile, head and neck tumours, lymphoma and myeloma; sarcoid makes 1,25-vitamin D. Pregnancy: placental 1,25-vitamin D raises urinary calcium; most stones pass.

q: Irreversible electroporation is attractive for central renal tumours mainly because it:
o: Needs no image guidance at all
e: IRE delivers electrical pulses via bipolar or monopolar electrodes that permeabilise membranes and kill cells while preserving scaffolding, large vessels and urothelium.

q: In idiopathic calcium oxalate formers, Randall plaques originate in the:
e: They are calcium apatite, extend subepithelially to the papilla and anchor calcium oxalate stones.

q: Which statement about spinal cord injury is FALSE?
o: DSD implies a lesion between pons and sacral cord
Sacral cord lies at about T12–L1 vertebrae
The bladder neck is open in spinal shock
The cord ends at about vertebral level L2
e: In spinal shock the bladder is areflexic, smooth-walled; the bladder neck is usually closed (unless prior surgery or thoracolumbar sympathetic injury); some sphincter EMG persists. Sacral cord begins at vertebral T12–L1; the cord ends near L2. Detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia requires a lesion between the pontine-mesencephalic centre and sacral cord, so it does not occur after stroke. DSD therapy eliminates sphincter activity or bypasses it (not sacral neuromodulation). Risk factors: overdistension, high storage pressure, high detrusor LPP, VUR, stones, infection; aim for low-pressure storage with CIC; avoid long-term prophylaxis in CIC.
b: DSD: lesion between pons and sacral cord

q: The ideal candidate for trimodal bladder-preserving therapy has:
o: A bulky T3b tumour with poor renal function
A small, solitary, fully resected T2
e: Ideal: solitary small T2, visibly complete TURBT, no hydronephrosis, normal renal function. Up to 15% have no residual tumour after TUR. pT0 at cystectomy confers a big survival benefit. Micropapillary variant is aggressive and chemo-poor; neuroendocrine tumours need neoadjuvant chemotherapy and surgery (paraneoplastic hypercortisolism, hypercalcaemia). MIBC is systemic: 80% present with it, up to 50% die, deaths from distant metastases within 2 years. Outcome factors: stage, performance status, LVI, age, sex, histology. After chemotherapy, metastases may appear in the CNS.

q: The antifibrotic effect of iNOS-derived nitric oxide in Peyronie disease is mainly through:
e: NO reacts with reactive oxygen species, reducing them, reduces myofibroblasts and collagen I; pentoxifylline is a nonspecific PDE inhibitor with similar aims.

q: Which inherited genes with moderate penetrance raise the risk of aggressive prostate cancer?
e: BRCA1, BRCA2 (strongest) and ATM are DNA damage repair genes. Many susceptibility loci on several chromosomes raise risk. PSMA (also expressed in brain and intestine) is a major imaging target.

q: Which statement about recurrent UTI in children is FALSE?
o: Boys over 1 year recur more than younger boys
ASB in a normal preschool girl needs no treatment
Bowel dysfunction raises UTI and VUR risk
e: An uneradicated nidus causes bacterial persistence, not reinfection. Recurrence: boys <1 year 18%, >1 year 32%; girls 26% and 40% (Winberg). Bladder-bowel dysfunction promotes UTI and VUR; treating constipation and voiding dysfunction reduces UTI and helps VUR resolve. Asymptomatic bacteriuria (0.8% of preschool girls) without VUR or anomalies needs no treatment. Women: early first UTI, maternal UTI and blood group antigens raise recurrence. Only 37% with DMSA-proven pyelonephritis have VUR (not 66%).
b: ASB in normal child: no treatment

q: Post-chemotherapy RPLND completely resects viable germ cell tumour. Next step:
e: Two more cycles improve survival when viable tumour is completely resected; prognosis depends on markers at RPLND, prior treatment and pathology.
b: Completely resected viable GCT: 2 cycles platinum

q: Which statement about collagenase Clostridium histolyticum (CCH) for PD is FALSE?
o: De novo ED is a common side effect
It was tested in stable 30–90° curves
e: IMPRESS phase 3: 17° vs 9° improvement in stable dorsal curves 30–90°, excluding hinge, calcification, hourglass, severe ED and ventral plaques; QoL improved. No de novo ED; bruising and pain are common and benign; fracture <1%. Main barriers: cost (book: $3300 per injection, 4 cycles of 2) and visits. Postoperative rehab (massage, stretch, nightly PDE5i, traction ≥3 h/day, dose-related) aims to preserve length, not contract the scar; traction does not harm sensation. Ideal graft does not contract. Note: CCH was withdrawn from the EU market in 2020 for commercial reasons.

q: Which statement about oxalate absorption is FALSE?
o: Low calcium intake cuts oxalate uptake
e: Low calcium intake increases oxalate absorption (less calcium-oxalate complex). O. formigenes uses oxalate as an energy source (not found in urine); H. pylori has no effect. Hyperoxaluria >40 mg/day; rich foods: nuts, chocolate, tea, spinach, broccoli, strawberries, rhubarb. Malabsorption (with intact colon): fatty acids bind calcium, bile salts raise colonic permeability. Roux-en-Y bypass: oxalate can exceed 100 mg/day. Calcium oxalate saturation depends equally on calcium and oxalate concentrations.
b: Low calcium intake raises oxalate uptake

q: The spinal cord ends at approximately vertebral level:
e: Sacral cord segments lie at vertebral T12–L1; below L2 lies the cauda equina.

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Disc prolapse gives areflexia with normal compliance
After pelvic surgery the smooth sphincter is often open
After pelvic surgery, start with CIC, not prostatectomy
Cauda equina syndrome causes limb spasticity
e: Cauda equina is lower motor neuron: perineal sensory loss, loss of voluntary sphincter control, sexual dysfunction, not spasticity. Disc protrusion: 27% areflexic with difficulty voiding; compliance usually normal. After radical pelvic surgery: impaired contractility, fixed striated tone ('obstruction'), open smooth sphincter, often low compliance, so stress incontinence with areflexia; most is transient; use CIC; prostatectomy may worsen incontinence. Diabetic bladder: impaired sensation, large capacity, poor contractility and flow, later residual. Bladder neck obstruction is localised by video-urodynamics.

q: Low urine pH in uric acid stone formers with diabetes is mainly due to:
e: Renal insulin resistance reduces ammonia production from glutamine and Na+/H+ exchanger activity, lowering urinary ammonium and pH; low pH is the key determinant of uric acid stones. Hyperuricosuria >600 mg/day. Uric acid stone formers have prolonged acid urine. Citric acid intake barely raises urinary citrate (absorbed citrate becomes bicarbonate neutralised by its proton); acid–base status determines citrate excretion (acidosis lowers it); hypocitraturia <320 mg/day.

q: After emptying the bladder, persistent autonomic dysreflexia is treated first with:
e: Remove the stimulus first; nitroglycerin vasodilates rapidly.

q: Which statement about Fowler syndrome is FALSE?
o: It affects young women with retention
Needle EMG shows a typical abnormality
Bladder capacity is usually under 1 L
e: Fowler syndrome: women usually under 30 with painless retention (capacity >1 L, no urgency), normal brain and spine MRI, characteristic urethral sphincter EMG activity. Hormones, drugs and botulinum toxin fail; neuromodulation works even after long retention. Mirabegron (β3) treats NDO without anticholinergic effects (may raise BP and heart rate slightly). Radiation: reduced capacity, low compliance, DO.

q: Which statement about bacterial virulence in UTI is FALSE?
o: Commensal bacteria can cause some UTIs
Flagella are not a virulence trait as such
Biofilm bacteria grow faster than usual
e: Biofilm bacteria grow slowly, which makes them antibiotic resistant. Virulence: pili, iron access, haemolysin, capsular polysaccharides, biofilms. Commensals cause a small share. LPS triggers Toll-like receptors (innate immunity: cytokines, chemokines, neutrophils). UTI raises renal pelvic pressure.
b: Flagella are not a virulence trait

q: Which does NOT by itself make a patient cisplatin-ineligible?
e: Ineligibility: poor performance status, CrCl <60 mL/min, hearing loss, peripheral neuropathy, heart failure. Age alone is not a criterion.
b: CrCl <60, poor PS, hearing loss, neuropathy, heart failure

q: Which statement about RTA and stones is FALSE?
o: Type 2 RTA is a distal H+-ATPase defect
Type 4 RTA occurs in diabetic renal damage
Distal RTA gives calcium phosphate stones
e: Type 1 (distal): defective H+-ATPase/H+ secretion; high urine pH, hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia, calcium phosphate stones; hypokalaemia. Type 2 (proximal): failed bicarbonate reabsorption. Type 4: aldosterone resistance in diabetics. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide, topiramate) act like RTA. Medullary sponge kidney: acidification defect, hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia.
b: Type 1: distal H+ secretion defect, CaP stones

q: Which statement about catheters and infection in children is FALSE?
o: CIC needs sterile catheters and prophylaxis
Catheters left over 4 days infect the urine
Catheter UTI is a leading nosocomial infection
e: For paediatric CIC neither sterile/single-use catheters nor prophylaxis is recommended; bacteriuria/pyuria (40–80%) is usually asymptomatic and untreated. Catheter UTI is the commonest paediatric nosocomial infection (book: second commonest overall; >1 million US cases/year); risk rises with duration; remove promptly; any catheter >4 days leads to infected urine.
b: No sterile catheters or prophylaxis for CIC

q: Compared with PSA, human kallikrein 2 (hK2) is:
e: PSA is intense in benign epithelium with minimal hK2; cancer tissue shows more hK2. hK2 cleaves proPSA to active PSA.
b: hK2 stronger in poorly differentiated cancer

q: Which pairing of situation and stone type is FALSE?
e: Laxative abuse (dehydration, intracellular acidosis, low urinary sodium) gives ammonium acid urate stones. Lesch-Nyhan (HGPRT deficiency) on high allopurinol accumulates xanthine (less soluble than hypoxanthine). Cystinuria: transport defect of cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine, but only cystine precipitates; autosomal recessive, two genes, types A, B, AB; up to 10% of stones in children. Urease producers: Proteus, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus (>90% of S. aureus). Drug stones: triamterene, silica, indinavir, ephedrine, ciprofloxacin. Horseshoe/UPJO stones: stasis plus metabolic factors.

q: Which statement about neurogenic bladder in children is FALSE?
o: About 90% of myelomeningocele have LUT dysfunction
Reflux can mask high bladder pressures
e: Myelomeningocele (usually lumbosacral): level correlates poorly with urodynamics; ~90% have LUT dysfunction; lifelong follow-up. Tethered cord: imaging does not correlate; detethering improves urodynamics in parallel with function. Significant reflux makes measured capacity larger and pressures lower (DO underestimated). Guillain-Barré: LUT dysfunction in 25–80%, usually reversible. Herpes zoster of sacral roots: retention, areflexia or DO (palm/sole rash suggests syphilis). Risk-stratify: treat if hydronephrosis, CKD, recurrent UTI or incontinence with skin problems.

q: According to the book, the commonest stone composition is:
e: Book: calcium oxalate 60%; mixed calcium oxalate/hydroxyapatite 20%; uric acid 10%; struvite 10%; brushite 2%; cystine 1%. Randall plaques (calcium apatite) start in the basement membrane of the thin loops of Henle and anchor calcium oxalate stones in idiopathic formers.

q: Which statement about long-term follow-up after renal scarring is TRUE?
o: Bilateral scars need BP and protein checks
e: Significant bilateral scars or reduced function: follow BP, renal function and proteinuria; proteinuria may hasten CKD and RAS blockade may slow it. Reflux nephropathy carries a 10–20% risk of hypertension; progressive deterioration with VUR routinely shows significant proteinuria.
b: Bilateral scars: lifelong BP, function, protein

q: Which urine culture result defines UTI?
e: Suprapubic aspiration is the most reliable: any growth. Catheter specimen ≥50,000 CFU/mL; clean catch ≥100,000 CFU/mL.
